en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Mahāvagga 10.
The Chapter on Kosambī (Kosambakakkhandhaka)
1. The Discourse on the Quarrel at Kosambī.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu had committed an offense.
Thus, he has the view that it is an offense regarding that offense,
while other monks have the view that it is not an offense regarding that offense.
At a later time, he comes to have the view that it is not an offense regarding that offense.
Other monks held the view that he had committed that offense.
Then those monks said to that monk, "Friend, you have committed an offense; do you see this offense?"
“There is no offense, friends, that I could see,” he said.
Then those monks, having achieved unanimity, suspended that monk for not recognizing an offense.

Now that monk was learned, one who had mastered the tradition, a bearer of the Dhamma, a bearer of the Vinaya, a bearer of the Mātikā; he was wise, competent, intelligent, conscientious, scrupulous, and desirous of training.
Then that bhikkhu approached the bhikkhus who were his friends and companions and said this:
“This is not an offense, friends; it is not an offense.
I have not committed an offense; I am not one who has committed an offense.”
"I have not been suspended; I am not suspended.
I was suspended by an illegal act—one that is reversible and unfit for the occasion.
May the venerable ones take my side according to the Dhamma and the Vinaya."
That bhikkhu indeed obtained a faction of bhikkhus who were his personal friends and associates.
He sent a messenger to the presence of those bhikkhus who were his personal friends and associates from the countryside, saying:
"Friends, this is not an offense; it is not an offense at all."
I am not one who has committed an offense;
I am not one who has fallen into an offense.
I have been suspended by a legal act that is contrary to the Dhamma, reversible, and unfit for the occasion.
“May the venerable ones side with me in accordance with the Dhamma and the Vinaya.
That bhikkhu then obtained as his supporters bhikkhus from the countryside who were both seen and associated with him.
Then those bhikkhus who followed the suspended one approached the bhikkhus who had carried out the suspension; having approached, they said this to the bhikkhus who had carried out the suspension:
“Friend, this is not an offense; it is not an offense at all.
This bhikkhu has not committed an offense; this bhikkhu has not fallen into an offense.
This bhikkhu has not been suspended; this bhikkhu has not been suspended.”
“He has been ejected by an illegitimate legal procedure—one that is reversible and not fit to stand.
When this was said, the monks who had carried out the ejection said to the monks who were following the one who had been ejected:
“This is an offense, friends; it is not a non-offense.”
This bhikkhu has committed an offense; this bhikkhu is not one who has not committed an offense.
This bhikkhu has been suspended; this bhikkhu is not one who has not been suspended.
He has been suspended by a legitimate legal act that is irreversible and fit to stand.
“Venerable sirs, do not follow or attend upon this suspended monk.
Even though those monks who followed the suspended monk were thus addressed by the monks who had suspended him, they continued to follow and attend upon that suspended monk in the same way.
Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, here a certain bhikkhu had fallen into an offense.
He held the view that it was an offense regarding that offense, while other bhikkhus held the view that it was not an offense regarding that same offense.”
Then, at a later time, he came to hold the view that there was no offense regarding that offense, while other monks held the view that there was an offense regarding that offense.
Then, venerable sir, those monks said this to that monk:
“Friend, you have fallen into an offense; do you see this offense?”
“‘I have no offense, friends, that I should see,’ he said.
Then, Bhante, those monks, having achieved unanimity, suspended that monk for not seeing his offense.

Yet, Bhante, that monk was learned, one who had mastered the tradition, a bearer of the Dhamma, a bearer of the Vinaya, a bearer of the Mātikā; he was wise, competent, intelligent, conscientious, scrupulous, and desirous of training.”
Then, venerable sir, that bhikkhu approached those bhikkhus who were his friends and companions and said this:
“This is not an offense, friends;
it is no offense.”
I am not one who has committed an offense; I am not one who has fallen into an offense.
I have been suspended by an illegal act—one that is reversible and unfit for its purpose.
"May the venerable ones become my faction in accordance with the Dhamma and the Vinaya.
And so, Bhante, that bhikkhu obtained a faction of bhikkhus who were his friends and associates.
He then sent a messenger to the presence of the bhikkhus who were his friends and associates from the countryside, saying:
‘This is not an offense, friend;
this is no offense.
I have not committed it; I am not one who has committed it.’
"I have not been suspended; I am not suspended.
I was suspended by a procedure that is contrary to the Dhamma, reversible, and unfit for the occasion.
May the venerable ones take my side according to the Dhamma and according to the Vinaya."
“Venerable sir, that bhikkhu indeed obtained as his faction bhikkhus from the countryside who were both seen and befriended by him.

Then, venerable sir, those bhikkhus who followed the one who had been suspended approached the bhikkhus who had carried out the suspension; having approached them, they said this to the bhikkhus who had carried out the suspension:
‘This is not an offense, friends.’”
This is not an offense.
This bhikkhu has not committed an offense; this bhikkhu is not one who has committed an offense.
This bhikkhu has not been suspended; this bhikkhu is not one who has been suspended.
“He has been suspended by an illegal act—one that is reversible and not fit to stand.
When this was said, Bhante, those monks who had carried out the suspension said to the monks who were following the suspended one:
“This is an offense, friends;”
This is not a non-offense.
This bhikkhu has committed an offense; this bhikkhu is not one who has not committed an offense.
This bhikkhu is suspended; this bhikkhu is not one who is not suspended.
“He has been suspended by a legal act that is in accordance with the Dhamma, irreversible, and fit to stand.
Venerable sirs, do not follow or attend upon this suspended monk!
Even though they were addressed in this way by the monks who had suspended him, those monks who followed the suspended one continued to follow and attend upon that suspended monk just as before.’”
Then the Blessed One, thinking, “The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is split! The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is split!

rose from his seat and approached the bhikkhus who were performing the suspension. Having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Sitting there, the Blessed One said this to the bhikkhus who were performing the suspension:
“Bhikkhus, do not think that a bhikkhu should be suspended for just any reason or another simply because it occurs to you, ‘It occurs to us; it occurs to us.’”
But here, monks, a monk has committed an offense.
He regards that offense as no offense, while other monks regard that offense as an offense.

If those monks know of that monk thus: ‘This venerable one is learned, of wide knowledge, one who has mastered the tradition, a bearer of the Dhamma, a bearer of the Vinaya, a bearer of the Mātikā, wise, competent, intelligent, conscientious, scrupulous, and desirous of training.’
“If we suspend this bhikkhu for not seeing an offense, we will not perform the Uposatha together with this bhikkhu; we will perform the Uposatha without this bhikkhu.
On that account, there will arise for the Saṅgha quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute, as well as schism in the Saṅgha, fracture in the Saṅgha, and division of the Saṅgha.”
“‘Causing a schism in the Saṅgha’: monks, that monk should not be suspended for his refusal to see an offense by monks who take the breaking of the Saṅgha seriously.
However, monks, there is the case where a monk has committed an offense.”
Thus he has the view that there is no offense for that offense, while the other monks have the view that there is an offense for that offense.

If those monks know of that monk thus: “This venerable one is learned, of wide knowledge, a bearer of the Dhamma, a bearer of the Vinaya, a bearer of the Mātikā; he is wise, competent, intelligent, conscientious, scrupulous, and desirous of training.
If we were to suspend this monk for not seeing an offense, we would not perform the invitation ceremony with this monk; we would perform the invitation ceremony without this monk.”
"We will not perform a formal act of the Saṅgha together with this bhikkhu; we will perform a formal act of the Saṅgha without this bhikkhu.
We will not sit on a seat together with this bhikkhu; we will sit on a seat without this bhikkhu.
We will not sit at the drinking of rice-gruel together with this bhikkhu; we will sit at the drinking of rice-gruel without this bhikkhu."
"We will not sit in the dining hall together with this monk; we will sit in the dining hall apart from this monk.
We will not dwell under the same roof together with this monk; we will dwell under the same roof apart from this monk.
We will not perform salutations, rising from our seats, or joining of palms in greeting according to seniority together with this monk."
"We shall perform the duties of propriety; without this monk, we shall perform the duties of propriety—such as salutation, rising to greet, and joining the palms—in accordance with seniority.
On account of this, there will arise for the Saṅgha quarreling, strife, contention, dispute, schism in the Saṅgha, and fracture in the Saṅgha."
‘The establishment of a separate Saṅgha, the division of the Saṅgha,’ monks, that monk should not be suspended for his refusal to see an offense by monks who take the gravity of schism seriously.
Then the Blessed One, having spoken this matter to the suspending monks, rose from his seat and went to those who followed the suspended monk.
The Blessed One approached those monks; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Once seated, the Blessed One said this to the monks who follow along with the suspension:
"Monks, having fallen into an offense, you should not think, 'We have not fallen into an offense; we have not fallen into an offense,' and thus fail to make amends for the offense.
For in this case, monks, a monk has fallen into an offense."
Thus, he has the view that there is no offense regarding that offense, while other monks have the view that there is an offense regarding that offense.
If, monks, that monk knows of those monks: “These venerable ones are learned, of inherited tradition, bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, bearers of the Mātikā;
they are wise, competent, intelligent, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training,” [he should act accordingly].
It is not right for me, whether on my own account or on account of others, to go astray through desire, hatred, delusion, or fear.
If these bhikkhus were to suspend me for not seeing an offense, they would not perform the Uposatha together with me;
they would perform the Uposatha without me. On that account, there would arise for the Saṅgha quarreling and strife.
‘Conflict, dispute, schism in the Saṅgha, strife in the Saṅgha, formal division of the Saṅgha,
and separation of the Saṅgha’— a monk who values harmony, monks, should confess his offense out of faith in others.
Furthermore, monks, there is the case where a monk has committed an offense.
Thus, he has the view that there is no offense regarding that offense, while the other bhikkhus have the view that there is an offense regarding that offense.
If, monks, that bhikkhu knows of those bhikkhus: “These venerable ones are learned, of inherited tradition, bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, bearers of the Mātikā;
they are wise, competent, intelligent, conscientious, scrupulous, and desirous of training,” [he should act accordingly].
It is not right for me, whether on my own account or on account of others, to go astray through desire, hatred, delusion, or fear.
If these bhikkhus suspend me for not seeing an offense, they will not perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) together with me; they will perform the invitation ceremony without me.
They will not carry out formal acts of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*) together with me; they will carry out formal acts of the Saṅgha without me.
They will not sit on a seat together with me; they will sit on a seat apart from me.
They will not sit together with me at the drinking of gruel; they will sit apart from me at the drinking of gruel.
They will not sit together with me in the dining hall; they will sit apart from me in the dining hall.
They will not live under one roof with me; they will live under one roof without me.
They will not perform salutations, rising from their seats, joining their palms, and respectful duties according to seniority while with me;
they will perform salutations, rising from their seats, joining their palms, and respectful duties according to seniority without me.
‘On account of this, there will arise for the Saṅgha quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute; a schism in the Saṅgha, a fracture in the Saṅgha,
a division in the Saṅgha, and a separation within the Saṅgha,’ then, monks,
a monk who values harmony should confess his offense even out of faith in others.”
Then the Blessed One, having spoken this matter to the monks who follow those who have been suspended, rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, the monks who followed those who had been suspended performed the Uposatha and carried out formal acts of the Saṅgha right there within the boundary (sīmā).
However, the monks who had carried out the suspension went outside the boundary to perform the Uposatha and carry out the formal acts of the Saṅgha.
Then a certain monk who was a follower of one suspended approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, that monk said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, those monks who follow one who has been suspended perform the Uposatha and carry out formal acts of the Saṅgha right there within the boundary."
"But we, the monks who have suspended them, shall go outside the boundary and perform the Uposatha and carry out the formal acts of the Saṅgha.
"If those monks who follow the suspended ones perform the Uposatha and carry out the formal acts of the Saṅgha right there within the boundary,
according to the motion and proclamations as laid down by me, then those formal acts of theirs— [are invalid]."
The formal acts will be legitimate, irreversible, and fit for the occasion.
If you, monks, who are the suspenders, perform the Uposatha and carry out the Sangha business right there within the boundary—
just as the motion and the proclamation have been prescribed by me— then those acts of yours will also be legitimate.
The legal acts will be unshakable and fit to stand.
Why is that? Because these monks belong to a different community from you, and you belong to a different community from them.
"Bhikkhu, there are these two grounds for being of a different communion:

either one makes oneself of a different communion by oneself, or a harmonious Saṅgha suspends one for not seeing [an offense], or for not making amends for it, or for not relinquishing [a wrong view].
These, bhikkhu, are the two grounds for being of a different communion."
“Monk, there are these two grounds for being of the same communion:

either one makes oneself of the same communion as oneself; or a harmonious Saṅgha reinstates one who has been suspended for not seeing [an offense], for not making amends, or for not relinquishing [a wrong view].
These, monk, are the two grounds for being of the same communion.”

Now at that time, monks, having become quarrelsome, contentious, and fallen into dispute in the dining hall within the village, displayed discordant bodily and verbal actions toward one another and engaged in physical shoving.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, having become quarrelsome, contentious, and fallen into dispute in the dining hall within the village..."
“Those involved in a dispute will engage in improper bodily and verbal actions toward one another; they will even go so far as to take each other’s hands.
The monks heard those people complaining, grumbling, and expressing their indignation.
Those monks who were of few desires complained, grumbled, and expressed their indignation.

“How indeed can monks, having become quarrelsome, contentious, and fallen into dispute in the dining hall or in a house, engage in improper bodily and verbal actions toward one another, and even touch each other’s hands?
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Blessed One asked:
“Is it true, monks, that monks, having become quarrelsome … in the dining hall or in a house … touch each other’s hands?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One,
rebuked him … Having rebuked him and given a Dhamma talk, he addressed the bhikkhus:

“Monks, when the Saṅgha is split and conducting itself unrighteously, behaving without mutual concord, one should sit down on a seat [thinking]: ‘To this extent we shall not engage in any improper bodily or verbal action toward one another, nor shall we touch hands.
Monks, when the Saṅgha is split but conducting itself righteously, behaving with mutual concord, one should sit down in the space between the seats.”
Now at that time, the monks were living in the midst of the Saṅgha quarreling, disputing, and falling into contention, stabbing one another with the weapons of their tongues.
They were unable to settle that legal issue.
Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, that monk said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, the bhikkhus in the midst of the Saṅgha have become engaged in quarrels, disputes, and contention; they dwell piercing one another with verbal darts.
They are unable to settle that legal issue.
It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would approach those bhikkhus out of compassion.”
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the Blessed One approached those bhikkhus; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said this to those bhikkhus:
“Enough, bhikkhus! No quarreling, no strife, no dispute, no contention.”
When this was said, a certain monk who spoke contrary to the Dhamma said this to the Blessed One:
“May the Blessed One wait, Lord;
may the Blessed One, the Master of the Dhamma, remain at ease, devoted to dwelling in happiness in this very life.”
“May we be known by this quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute.
A second time, the Blessed One said to those bhikkhus:
“Enough, bhikkhus! No more quarreling, no more strife, no more contention, no more dispute.”
A second time, that monk who spoke contrary to the Dhamma said this to the Blessed One:
“May the Blessed One wait, Lord;
may the Blessed One, the Master of the Dhamma, remain at ease, devoted to dwelling in the happiness of the Dhamma in this very life.”
“May we be known by this quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute.
2. The Story of Dīghāvu:
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:

“Once upon a time, monks, there was a king of Kāsi in Bārāṇasī named Brahmadatta, who was wealthy, with great riches, great possessions, great power, many mounts, and vast conquests; his treasury and granaries were full.
There was also a king of Kosala named Dīghīti, who was poor, with little wealth, little possessions, little power, few mounts, and little conquest; his treasury and granaries were not full.
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi, having arrayed a fourfold army, marched out against King Dīghīti of Kosala.”
“Bhikkhus, King Dīghīti of Kosala heard: ‘It is said that Brahmadatta, the King of Kāsi, having arrayed his fourfold army, has marched out against me.

Then, bhikkhus, it occurred to King Dīghīti of Kosala: ‘King Brahmadatta of Kāsi is wealthy, of great riches, of great possessions, of great power, with many mounts, a great conqueror, and his treasuries and storehouses are full; whereas I—’”
“In Pañcāla I am poor, with little property, little wealth, little power, few vehicles, and no conquered territories; my treasuries and granaries are not full.
I am not capable of even joining forces for a single battle with Brahmadatta, the King of Kāsi.
What if I were to depart from the city beforehand?”
Then, monks, King Dīghīti of Kosala took his chief queen and fled from the city beforehand.
Then, monks, Brahmadatta, the King of Kāsi, having completely conquered King Dīghīti of Kosala’s army, vehicles, territory, treasury, and granaries, took up residence there.
Thereupon, monks, King Dīghīti of Kosala set out for Benares together with his wife.

Gradually, he arrived at Bārāṇasī. There, monks, King Dīghīti of Kosala, together with his queen, was dwelling in Bārāṇasī in a certain outlying area, in the residence of a potter, disguised as a stranger under the cloak of a wanderer.
Then, monks, not long after, the chief consort of King Dīghīti of Kosala became pregnant.

A pregnancy craving such as this arose in her: she desired to see a fourfold army, clad in armor and standing on level ground, at the time of sunrise, and to drink the water used for washing their swords.
Then, monks, the chief queen of King Dīghīti of Kosala said this to King Dīghīti of Kosala:
“I am pregnant, Your Majesty. A pregnancy craving such as this has arisen in me—I desire to see a fourfold army at the time of sunrise...”
"To see an army arrayed in armor standing on level ground upon an anthill, and to drink the rinsing of their swords.
"From where, O Queen, could we—who are so wretched—obtain a fourfold army arrayed in armor standing on level ground upon an anthill, or the rinsing of swords?
"If I do not obtain this, O King, I shall die."
Now at that time, monks, the brahmin chaplain of Brahmadatta, the king of Kāsi, was a friend of Dīghīti, the king of Kosala.

Then, monks, King Dīghīti of Kosala approached the brahmin chaplain of Brahmadatta, the king of Kāsi, and having approached him, he said this to the brahmin chaplain of Brahmadatta, the king of Kāsi: "Friend..."
“Sir, she is pregnant.
Such a craving has arisen in her: she wishes, at the time of sunrise, to see a fourfold army arrayed in mail standing on level ground, and to drink the water used for washing their swords.
“In that case, Your Majesty, let us go and see the queen as well.”
Then, monks, the chief queen of King Dīghīti of Kosala approached the brahmin chaplain of King Brahmadatta of Kāsi.
When the brahmin chaplain of King Brahmadatta of Kāsi saw the chief queen of King Dīghīti of Kosala coming from afar,
he rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and went toward her.
The chief queen of King Dīghīti of Kosala, having extended her joined palms in reverence, uttered this inspired exclamation three times:
“O, the King of Kosala is indeed in my womb! O, the King of Kosala is indeed in my womb!
“Be joyful, O Queen.”
"You will be able to see at the time of sunrise a fourfold army arrayed in armor standing on level ground, and you will be able to drink the water used for washing their swords.
Then, monks, the brahmin family priest of Brahmadatta, the King of Kāsi, approached King Brahmadatta of Kāsi; having approached, he said this to King Brahmadatta of Kāsi:
“‘In that way, Your Majesty, omens are seen; tomorrow at sunrise, let the fourfold army stand armored on level ground, and let the swords be washed.
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi gave orders to his men: ‘Men, do exactly as the brahmin household priest has said.’”

"Bhikkhus, the chief queen of King Dīghīti of Kosala obtained the opportunity to see a fourfold army, armored and arrayed on level ground, at the time of sunrise, and to drink the water used for washing their swords.
Then, bhikkhus, as that pregnancy reached maturity, the chief queen of King Dīghīti of Kosala gave birth to a son.
They gave him the name Dīghāvu."
Then, monks, before long, Prince Dīghāvu reached the age of discretion.
Then, monks, it occurred to King Dīghīti of Kosala: ‘This Brahmadatta, King of Kāsi, has done us much harm;
by him our army, our vehicles, our territory, and our treasury [have been seized].’
"And the storehouse has been seized. If he learns of this, he will surely have all three of us executed.
What if I were to have Prince Dīghāvu reside outside the city?
Then, monks, King Dīghīti of Kosala had Prince Dīghāvu reside outside the city.
Then, monks, while staying outside the city, Prince Dīghāvu learned all the crafts before long.
Now at that time, King Dīghīti of Kosala’s barber was living with King Brahmadatta of Kāsi.
Monks, the barber of King Dīghīti of Kosala saw King Dīghīti of Kosala together with his queen.
In Bārāṇasī, while staying in a certain outlying place in the dwelling of a potter under the disguise of a wanderer and in an unknown guise,
[the Blessed One] was seen. Having seen him, he approached Brahmadatta, the King of Kāsī, and having approached,
he said this to Brahmadatta, the King of Kāsī:

“‘Dīghīti, Your Majesty, King of Kosala, together with his queen, is living in Bārāṇasī in a certain outlying place, in the dwelling of a potter, disguised as a stranger and wearing the cloak of a wanderer.
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi gave orders to his men: ‘Well then, my good men, bring King Dīghīti of Kosala here, together with his queen.
‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ those men replied to King Brahmadatta of Kāsi, and they brought King Dīghīti of Kosala there, together with his queen.”
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi gave orders to his men:
“In that case, my men, bind King Dīghīti of Kosala and his wife with strong ropes behind their backs,
shave their heads, and lead them from street to street to the beat of a harsh-sounding drum.”
‘Having led him from street to street, have him exit through the southern gate;
then, having cut the city into four parts to the south, bury the corpses in pits in the four directions.
‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ those men replied to Brahmadatta, the King of Kāsi, and they [did so with] Dīghīti.

“Having bound the King of Kosala and his queen with strong ropes, pinioning their arms behind their backs, shaving their heads, and making them march from street to street, from crossroads to crossroads to the beat of a harsh-sounding drum, they paraded them about.
Then, monks, it occurred to Prince Dīghāvu: ‘I have not seen my mother and father for a long time. What if I were to go see them?’”
Then, monks, Prince Dīghāvu, having entered Bārāṇasī,
saw his parents with their arms tightly bound behind their backs with a strong rope, their heads shaved,
being led from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads to the accompaniment of a harsh-sounding drum; seeing them, he approached where his parents were.
“Monks, King Dīghīti of Kosala saw Prince Dīghāvu coming from afar; having seen him, he said to Prince Dīghāvu:
‘Do not look for the long, my dear Dīghāvu, nor for the short.
For, my dear Dīghāvu, hostilities are not appeased by hostility.’”
“Indeed, dear Dīghāvu, it is through non-enmity that enmities are appeased.
When this was said, monks, those people said to King Dīghīti of Kosala: “This King Dīghīti of Kosala is mad; he is raving.
Who is this ‘Dīghāvu’ of his?”
Who is it that says this to you: “Do not look for the long, dear Dīghāvu, nor for the short.
For, dear Dīghāvu, enmities are not settled by enmity;
rather, dear Dīghāvu, enmities are settled by non-enmity”?
“‘I am not mad, my man,’ he said, ‘nor do I speak incoherently; rather, whoever is wise will understand.
A second time, monks...
and a third time, monks, King Dīghīti of Kosala said this to Prince Dīghāvu:”
‘Do not look long, dear Dīghāvu, nor look short.
For, dear Dīghāvu, hatreds are not appeased by hatred;
rather, dear Dīghāvu, hatreds are appeased by non-hatred.’
A third time, monks, those people said this to King Dīghīti of Kosala:
"This King Dīghīti of Kosala is mad; he is raving.
Who is this Dīghāvu?"
To whom did he speak thus:
"Do not look long, dear Dīghāvu, do not look short.
For, dear Dīghāvu, hostilities are not appeased by hostility."
“Indeed, dear Dīghāvu, it is through non-enmity that enmities are appeased.
“I am not mad, my friend, nor do I speak incoherently; rather, the wise will understand this.
Then, monks, those people [dragged] King Dīghīti of Kosala and his queen from street to street...
Having led him from street to street, they brought him out through the southern gate;
having cut the city into four parts to the south, they placed pits in the four directions, stationed guards, and departed.
Then, monks, Prince Dīghāvu entered Bārāṇasī, took out the liquor, and made the guards drink it.

When they had become intoxicated and fallen down, Prince Dīghāvu gathered wood, prepared a funeral pyre, placed the bodies of his parents upon the pyre, set fire to it, and with palms joined in reverence, circumambulated the pyre three times.
Now at that time, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi was situated on the upper terrace of his palace.
King Brahmadatta of Kāsi saw Prince Dīghāvu circumambulating the pyre three times with palms joined in reverence; having seen him, this thought occurred to him:
“Without a doubt, that man must be a kinsman or a blood relative of King Dīghīti of Kosala; alas, I am undone, for no one indeed has informed me!

Then, monks, Prince Dīghāvu went into the forest and, having wept and cried his fill, wiped away his tears, entered Bārāṇasī, went to the elephant stable near the inner palace, and said this to the elephant trainer:
“I wish, teacher, to learn a craft.
“In that case, my dear young man, you may learn it.
Then, monks, at the time of dawn, Prince Dīghāvu would rise and sing with a sweet voice in the elephant stable and play the lute.

Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi, having risen at the time of dawn during the night, heard a sweet voice singing and the playing of a lute in the elephant stable. Upon hearing it, he asked his men:
“Tell me, who is this that has risen at the time of dawn during the night and is singing with a sweet voice and playing the lute in the elephant stable?

“Sire, it is a young brahmin student, a pupil of such-and-such an elephant trainer, who has risen at the time of dawn during the night and is singing with a sweet voice and playing the lute in the elephant stable.”
"In that case, my good man, bring that young man here.
"Yes, Your Majesty," those men replied to Brahmadatta, the King of Kāsi, and they brought Prince Dīghāvu. [The king asked:
"My good man, young man, did you rise at the break of dawn during the night and sing in a sweet voice and play the lute in the elephant stable?"
‘“So be it, Your Majesty,” he replied.
“In that case, my dear young man, sing and play the lute.
“So be it, Your Majesty,” the prince Dīghāvu replied to King Brahmadatta of Kāsi, and with a desire to please him, he sang in a sweet voice and played the lute.’
“‘Boy, my lad, you attend upon me,’ he said.
‘Yes, sire,’ the prince Dīghāvu replied to Brahmadatta, the King of Kāsi.
Then, monks, Prince Dīghāvu rose before King Brahmadatta and retired after him; he was one who accepted his duties, behaved agreeably, and spoke kindly.”
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsī soon established Prince Dīghāvu in a position of intimate trust within his inner circle.
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsī said this to Prince Dīghāvu:
“In that case, my dear young man, have the chariot harnessed; we shall go hunting.”
‘So be it, Your Majesty,’ the prince Dīghāvu replied to Brahmadatta, the King of Kāsi. Having harnessed the chariot, he said to King Brahmadatta of Kāsi, ‘Your Majesty, the chariot is ready;
now please do as you deem fit. Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi mounted the chariot.
Prince Dīghāvu drove the chariot;
he drove it in such a way that the army went by one path while the chariot went by another.
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsī, having traveled a great distance, said this to Prince Dīghāvu:
"In that case, my dear young man, unyoke the chariot; I am weary and shall lie down.
"Very well, Your Majesty," the prince Dīghāvu replied to Brahmadatta, the King of Kāsi. Having unyoked the chariot, he sat down cross-legged upon the ground.
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi lay down with his head in the lap of Prince Dīghāvu.
As he was exhausted, sleep fell upon him in an instant.
Then, monks, it occurred to Prince Dīghāvu:
“This Brahmadatta, King of Kāsi, has done us much harm.”
‘By him our army, our mounts, our territory, our treasury, and our granaries have been seized;
by him my parents have been killed.
This indeed is the time for me to repay his enmity. With these words, he drew his sword from its scabbard.
Then, monks, it occurred to Prince Dīghāvu:
"At the time of his death, my father said to me: 'Do not look for the long, dear Dīghāvu, nor for the short.
For, dear Dīghāvu, hostilities are not appeased by hostility.'"
“Indeed, dear Dīghāvu, it is through non-enmity that enmities are appeased.
“It would not be fitting for me to transgress my father’s word,” he thought, and he sheathed his sword in its scabbard.
A second time, monks, this occurred to Prince Dīghāvu:
“This King Brahmadatta of Kāsi has indeed done us much harm;
by him our army, our vehicles, our territory, our treasury, and our storehouses were seized, and by him my parents were killed.
This is the time for me to repay his enmity,” he thought, and he drew his sword from its scabbard.
A second time, monks, this occurred to Prince Dīghāvu:
"At the time of his death, my father said to me: 'My dear Dīghāvu, do not look for the long, nor for the short; for, my dear Dīghāvu, enmities are not stilled by enmity;
rather, my dear Dīghāvu, enmities are stilled by non-enmity.'"
‘It would not be fitting for me to transgress my father’s word,’ he thought.
He then inserted the sword back into the sheath.
And a third time, monks, this occurred to Prince Dīghāvu:
“This King Brahmadatta of Kāsi has indeed done us much harm.
By him our army, our mounts, our territory, our treasury, and our granaries have been seized;
and by him my parents were killed.”
“This is the time for me to strike back at my enemy,” he thought, and he drew his sword from its scabbard made of kosiya silk.
For a third time, monks, it occurred to Prince Dīghāvu:
“At the time of his death, my father said to me: ‘My dear Dīghāvu, do not look for what is long, nor for what is short.’”
“Indeed not, dear Dīghāvu; for enmities are not settled by enmity. Rather, dear Dīghāvu, enmities are settled by non-enmity.
“It would not be fitting for me to transgress my father’s word,” he said, and he once again sheathed his sword in its scabbard.
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi, terrified, agitated, apprehensive, and trembling, rose up in haste.
Then, monks, Prince Dīghāvu said this to King Brahmadatta of Kāsi: “Why, sire, have you risen up in haste, terrified, agitated, apprehensive, and trembling?
“It was just now, my boy, that Prince Dīghāvu, the son of King Dīghīti of Kosala, struck me down with a sword in a dream.”
"Therefore, terrified, agitated, apprehensive, and trembling, I rose up in haste.
Then, monks, Prince Dīghāvu, having touched the head of King Brahmadatta of Kāsi with his left hand and unsheathed his sword with his right hand, said this to King Brahmadatta of Kāsi:
"I am indeed that Prince Dīghāvu, the son of King Dīghīti of Kosala, O Lord."
"You have done us much harm.
By you our army, our mounts, our country, our treasury, and our granaries were seized;
and by you my mother and father were killed."
‘This indeed is the time for me to take revenge.
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi fell with his head at the feet of Prince Dīghāvu and said this to him:
‘Give me my life back, dear Dīghāvu! Give me my life back, dear Dīghāvu!’”
“‘Am I able to give my life for the sake of the King?
The King, indeed, would give his life for mine.
‘In that case, dear Dīghāvu, you give me your life, and I shall give you my life.’”
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi and Prince Dīghāvu gave each other their lives, took each other’s hands, and made an oath against treachery.
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi said this to Prince Dīghāvu:
“In that case, dear Dīghāvu, harness the chariot; we shall go.”
“‘So be it, Your Majesty,’ the prince Dīghāvu replied to Brahmadatta, the King of Kāsi. Having harnessed the chariot, he said to King Brahmadatta of Kāsi, ‘Your Majesty, the chariot is ready;
you may go at whatever time you deem fit.
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi mounted the chariot.”
Prince Dīghāvu drove the chariot;
he drove it in such a way that before long it had joined the army.
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi, having entered Bārāṇasī, summoned his ministers and counselors and said this to them:
“If, sirs, you were to see Prince Dīghāvu, the son of King Dīghīti of Kosala, what would you do to him?
Some said, “Your Majesty, we would cut off his hands.”
"Your Majesty, we would cut off our feet.
Your Majesty, we would cut off our hands and feet.
Your Majesty, we would cut off our ears."
‘We would cut off our nose, O King;
we would cut off our ears and nose, O King;
we would cut off our heads, O King.’”
“This, my man, is Prince Dīghāvu, the son of King Dīghīti of Kosala.
It is not possible to do anything to him.
He has given me my life, and I have given him his life.”
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi said this to Prince Dīghāvu:
“What your father, dear Dīghāvu, said at the time of his death was: ‘Do not look for the long, dear Dīghāvu, nor for the short.
For, dear Dīghāvu, hostilities are not appeased by hostility.’”
“‘For by non-enmity, dear Dīghāvu, enmities are settled’—what did your father mean when he said this?
“Your majesty, when my father spoke at the time of his death, saying ‘Not long,’ he meant: ‘Do not harbor enmity for long.
Your majesty, it was this that my father said at the time of his death: ‘Not long.’”
“O King, what my father said to me at the time of his death was: ‘Do not be hasty,’ meaning: ‘Do not be quick to break with your friends.
This is what my father said to me at the time of his death: ‘Do not be hasty.

And what my father said to me at the time of his death was: ‘For enmity, dear Dīghāvu, is not settled by enmity; rather, dear Dīghāvu, enmities are settled by non-enmity. It was by you, O King, that my parents were killed.”
If I were to deprive the King of life, those who wish him well would deprive me of life, and those who wish me well would deprive them of life—
in this way, that enmity would not be appeased by enmity.
But now the King has granted me my life, and I have granted the King his life.
"Thus is that enmity stilled by non-enmity.
Your father said this to me, O King, at the time of his death:
'For indeed, dear Dīghāvu, enmities are not stilled by enmity;'"
“Indeed, dear Dīghāvu, it is through non-enmity that enmities are settled.
Then, monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsī thought:
“How wonderful, indeed! How marvelous, indeed!”
"How wise this Prince Dīghāvu is, in that he understands in detail the meaning of what his father spoke in brief!
Thus [the king] handed over to him his paternal army, vehicles, territory, treasury, and granary,
and gave him his daughter in marriage.
“Bhikkhus, such patience and gentleness will indeed belong even to those kings who have taken up the rod and taken up the sword!
But in this case, bhikkhus, it would be fitting for you who have gone forth in such a well-expounded Dhamma and Discipline to be patient and gentle.
A third time, the Blessed One said this to those bhikkhus:
“Enough, monks! No quarreling, no strife, no dispute, no contention!
For a third time, that monk who spoke contrary to the Dhamma said this to the Blessed One:
“May the Blessed One wait, Lord, Master of the Dhamma;”
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One dwell at ease, devoted to a pleasant abiding in this very life;
we shall be known by this quarrel, dispute, contention, and strife.
Then the Blessed One—
“These foolish men are consumed by their own forms; it is not easy to convince them.
Having said this, he rose from his seat and departed.
The first section on the discourse with Dīghāvu is finished.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Kosambī for alms.

Having walked for alms in Kosambī, after his meal, on his return from the alms round, he put away his lodging, took his bowl and robe, and while standing in the midst of the Saṅgha, he uttered these verses:
“The crowd is loud, the people are gathered;”
When the Saṅgha is being split, let no one think "I am a fool," nor should they think anything else more [important].
Those who appear wise but are utterly deluded,
speaking only within the range of mere words,
will stretch out their mouths as far as they desire.
The wise do not understand that by which they are led:
"He abused me, he struck me,
he defeated me, he robbed me."
And those who harbor resentment toward such a person find that their enmity is not appeased. "He reviled me,
he struck me," [they think].
"He has conquered me, he has defeated me";
yet for those who do not harbor resentment toward him,
their enmity subsides.
For hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world;
it is appeased only by non-hatred.
This is the eternal law.
Others do not understand it,
yet we strive for it here.
And those who understand this therein,
from that their quarrels are stilled—
those who break the bones and take away life.
Those who carry off cattle, horses, and wealth,
plundering the kingdom—
they too come together.
Why should it not be so for you?
If one should find a wise companion,
a steadfast friend who walks with one and dwells in virtue;
Having overcome all dangers,
one should wander with a joyful mind and mindfulness.
If one does not find a wise companion, [one should wander alone].
Having abandoned a wise companion who lives rightly and practices well—
just as a king leaves behind a conquered kingdom—
one should wander alone like a tusker elephant in the forest.
The life of one who wanders alone is better;
there is no companionship with a fool.
One should wander alone and commit no evil deeds.
“Free from anxiety, like an elephant in the Mātaṅga forest.
Then the Blessed One, having spoken these verses while standing in the midst of the Saṅgha, approached the village of Bālakaloṇaka.
Now at that time, the Venerable Bhagu was dwelling in the village of Bālakaloṇakagāma.

The Venerable Bhagu saw the Blessed One coming from afar; having seen him, he prepared a seat, set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone, and going forth to meet him, he received his bowl and robe.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat, and having sat down, he washed his feet.
The Venerable Bhagu, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Bhagu was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"I hope, monk, that you are bearing up; I hope you are getting by."
“I hope you are keeping well; I hope you are not suffering from lack of almsfood?
“It is bearable, Blessed One; I am keeping well, Blessed One;
and I am not suffering from lack of almsfood, Bhante.”
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the Venerable Bhagu with a discourse on the Dhamma,
rose from his seat and went to the Eastern Bamboo Park.
Now at that time, the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila were dwelling in the Eastern Bamboo Park.
The park keeper saw the Blessed One coming from afar; having seen him, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Do not enter this park, ascetic.
There are three sons of good family staying here who dwell intent on their own welfare."
“Do not cause them any inconvenience.
The Venerable Anuruddha overheard the park keeper conversing with the Blessed One, and having heard this, he said to the park keeper:
“Friend park keeper, do not obstruct the Blessed One.”
“The Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.
Then the Venerable Anuruddha approached the Venerable Nandiya and the Venerable Kimila; having approached, he said this to the Venerable Nandiya and the Venerable Kimila:
“Come forward, venerable sirs, come forward! The Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.”
Then the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila went out to meet the Blessed One;
one received the Blessed One’s bowl and robes, one prepared a seat, and one set out water for washing the feet,
a footstool, and a foot-washing stone.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat; having sat down, he washed his feet.
Those venerable ones, too, paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As the venerable Anuruddha was sitting there to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“I hope it is bearable for you, Anuruddhas; I hope you are getting by;
I hope you are not distressed by lack of almsfood?
“It is bearable, Blessed One; we are getting by, Blessed One.”
“And we are not troubled for lack of alms-food, venerable sir.
“But, Anuruddhas, do you dwell in harmony, cordial, without dispute, like milk and water, viewing one another with eyes of affection?
“Indeed, venerable sir, we dwell in harmony, cordial, without dispute, like milk and water, viewing one another with eyes of affection.”
“But how is it, Anuruddhas, that you dwell in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, like milk and water, regarding one another with eyes of love?
“Here, venerable sir, this thought occurs to me:
‘It is a gain for me, truly a great gain for me, that I dwell together with such fellow-practitioners of the holy life.’”
Venerable sir, toward these venerable ones, I maintain loving bodily action both openly and in private;
I maintain loving verbal action...
and I maintain loving mental action both openly and in private.
“Venerable sir, it occurred to me:
‘What if I were to set aside my own mind and conduct myself according to the minds of these very venerable ones?
And so, venerable sir, having set aside my own mind, I conduct myself according to the minds of these very venerable ones.”
“Indeed, venerable sir, our bodies are many, but our minds, I think, are one.
Then the Venerable Nandiya...
[and] the Venerable Kimila also said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it occurs to me too:
‘It is indeed a gain for me, it is indeed a great fortune for me, that I dwell together with such fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Venerable sir, toward these venerable ones, I maintain acts of loving-kindness through my body, both openly and in private.”
“Bhante, I maintain loving verbal action and loving mental action both openly and in private.
Then, Bhante, it occurs to me:
‘What if I were to set aside my own mind and conduct myself according to the minds of these venerable ones?’”
“Thus, venerable sir, having set aside my own mind, I conduct myself according to the minds of these very venerable ones.
For indeed, venerable sir, we have different bodies, yet it seems to me there is but one mind.
In this way, venerable sir, we dwell in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, like milk and water mixed together, regarding one another with eyes of love.”
“But, Anuruddhas, do you dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute?
“Indeed, Bhante, we dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute.
“But in what way, Anuruddhas, do you dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute?”
“Here, venerable sir, whichever one among us returns first from the village with almsfood prepares a seat, sets out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-stand;
having washed the bowl for leftover scraps, he places it there;
and he sets out drinking water and water for rinsing.

When he returns from the village for alms, if there is food remaining from his meal and he wishes to eat it, he does so; if he does not wish to eat it, he discards it where there is little vegetation or he throws it into water that contains no living beings.

He puts away his seat, puts away the foot-stool, the foot-stand, and the foot-washing stone; having washed the bowl for scraps, he puts it away; he puts away the drinking water and the water for washing; and he sweeps the dining hall.
If anyone sees that the water jar, the drinking jar, or the toilet jar is empty or void, he refills it.

If it is too heavy for him to carry, he calls a second person by a gesture of the hand and refills it by passing it from hand to hand; yet, venerable sir, we do not break out into speech on that account.
Furthermore, venerable sir, every five days we sit together all night long engaged in Dhamma discussion.
“In this way, Bhante, we dwell heedful, ardent, and resolute.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila regarding the journey to Pālileyyaka.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma,
he rose from his seat and set out on a wandering tour toward Pārileyyaka.
Wandering by stages on his tour, he eventually arrived at Pārileyyaka.
There, the Blessed One was dwelling at Pārileyyaka in the Protected Grove, at the foot of the Bhaddasāla tree.
Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:

"Formerly, I lived in discomfort, crowded by those monks of Kosambī who were makers of strife, makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, makers of contention, and makers of legal issues within the Saṅgha."

"I am now living alone, without a companion, in happiness and comfort, apart from those monks of Kosambī who are makers of strife, makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, makers of contention, and creators of legal issues within the Saṅgha.
And another great bull elephant lived surrounded by male elephants, female elephants, calf-elephants, and baby elephants;
he ate grass with its tips cut off, while they ate his broken-off branches, and the water was turbid.
He drank water, and as he had entered the bathing pool, female elephants went by, rubbing their bodies against his.
Then it occurred to that lordly elephant:
"I am indeed living crowded with male elephants, female elephants, elephant calves, and elephant cubs; [the grass] has its tips broken off..."
"I eat only grass; others eat my broken-off branches. I drink turbid water;
when I have entered a bathing pool, female elephants come along rubbing their bodies against mine.
What if I were to dwell alone, withdrawn from the herd?"
Then that noble elephant, having departed from the herd, approached Pālileyyaka, the protected forest grove; he went to the foot of the auspicious *sāla* tree where the Blessed One was,
and having approached, he offered drinking water and washing water to the Blessed One with his trunk and cleared away the overgrown grass.
Then it occurred to that noble elephant:
"Formerly, being crowded by other elephants, female elephants, male calves, and baby elephants, I did not dwell in comfort;
I had to eat grass with its tips broken off, and they ate away my broken-off branches, making them muddy."
"I drank water and, when I had plunged into the pools, female elephants came along rubbing their bodies against mine.
But now, alone and without a companion, I dwell in happiness and comfort, apart from the male elephants, the females, the calves, and the baby elephants.

Then the Blessed One, having understood his own seclusion and having known with his own mind the reflection in the mind of that lordly elephant, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation (udāna): "Truly, for one who has cut off all ties, Who has severed all bonds, For whom there is no more 'mine,' There is no longing anywhere."
“The mind of this Naga,
the elephant with tusks like chariot-poles,
is equal to [the mind] of that [other] elephant through the mind.”
“When one finds delight alone in the forest.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Pārileyyaka for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Sāvatthī.
Traveling by stages on his tour, he eventually arrived at Sāvatthī.
There the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the lay followers of Kosambī thought:
“These venerable Kosambī bhikkhus have done us much harm.”
“Harassed by these [monks], the Blessed One has departed.
Come now, noble ladies, let us neither salute the monks of Kosambī, nor rise for them, nor perform the añjali-greeting or the proper rites of hospitality;
let us neither honor them, nor revere them, nor esteem them, nor associate with them.”
"We will not honor them; even when they approach us, we will not give them alms-food.
Thus, being unhonored, unrespected, undervalued, excluded from our community, unworshipped, and treated with disrespect by us, they will either depart, disrobe, or win over the Blessed One.
Then the lay followers of Kosambī neither saluted the monks of Kosambī nor rose for them.
They performed the salutation with joined palms and the duties of respect, yet they did not honor him, did not revere him, did not esteem him, did not associate with him, and did not worship him;
nor did they give alms even to those who had approached them.
Then the monks of Kosambī, being unhonored, unrevered, unesteemed, unassociated with, and unworshiped by the lay followers of Kosambī, and being treated with such disrespect, spoke thus:
“Come, friends, let us go to Sāvatthī and settle this legal dispute in the presence of the Blessed One.
Then the Kosambī monks, having put their lodgings in order and taking their bowls and robes, set out for Sāvatthī.
The Venerable Sāriputta heard:
“It seems that those monks of Kosambī—who are makers of strife, makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, makers of contention, and creators of legal issues in the Saṅgha—are coming to Sāvatthī.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting to one side, he said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, it is said that those Kosambī monks—who are makers of strife, makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, makers of contention, and creators of legal issues in the Saṅgha—are coming to Sāvatthī.
How, venerable sir, should I conduct myself toward those monks?”
“In that case, Sāriputta, stand in accordance with the Dhamma.
“But how, Bhante, shall I know what is the Dhamma and what is not the Dhamma?
“Sāriputta, one who speaks contrary to the Dhamma is to be known by eighteen grounds.”
Here, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu proclaims what is not Dhamma as Dhamma,
and proclaims what is Dhamma as not Dhamma;
he proclaims what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, and...
He proclaims what is discipline as non-discipline;
he proclaims what was not spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata as having been spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata,
and he proclaims what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata as not having been spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata.
He proclaims what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as having been practiced by the Tathāgata,
and he proclaims what was practiced by the Tathāgata as not having been practiced by the Tathāgata;
he proclaims what was not laid down by the Tathāgata as having been laid down by the Tathāgata.
He proclaims what was laid down by the Tathāgata as not laid down by the Tathāgata;
he proclaims a non-offense as an offense, and an offense as a non-offense.
He represents a light offense as a heavy offense,
he represents a heavy offense as a light offense;
he represents an offense with remainder as an offense without remainder.
He represents an offense without remainder as an offense with remainder;
he represents a grave offense as a non-grave offense,
and he represents a non-grave offense as a grave offense.
By these eighteen grounds, Sāriputta, one who speaks contrary to the Dhamma is to be known.
And by eighteen grounds, Sāriputta, one who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma is to be known.
Here, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu proclaims what is contrary to the Dhamma as "contrary to the Dhamma."
He proclaims what is Dhamma as "Dhamma";
he proclaims what is non-discipline as "non-discipline," and he proclaims discipline as "discipline."

He proclaims that which was not spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata as "not spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata," and he proclaims that which was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata as "spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata";
he proclaims that which was not practiced by the Tathāgata as "not practiced by the Tathāgata."
He proclaims what was practiced by the Tathāgata as "practiced by the Tathāgata";
he proclaims what was not prescribed by the Tathāgata as "not prescribed by the Tathāgata," and he proclaims what was prescribed by the Tathāgata as "prescribed by the Tathāgata."
He explains what is not an offense as "not an offense," and he explains what is an offense as "an offense";
he explains a light offense as "a light offense."
He explains a grave offense as a grave offense;
he explains an offense with remainder as an offense with remainder,
and he explains an offense without remainder as an offense without remainder.
He proclaims a grave offense as a grave offense,
and he proclaims a non-grave offense as a non-grave offense—
it is by these eighteen grounds, Sāriputta, that one who speaks according to the Dhamma is to be known.”
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna heard...
[and so on] ...the Venerable Mahākassapa heard...
the Venerable Mahākaccāna heard...
The Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika heard...
The Venerable Mahākappina heard...
The Venerable Mahācunda heard...
The Venerable Anuruddha heard;
the Venerable Revata heard;

Then the Venerable Rāhula approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the Venerable Rāhula said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, it is said that those monks of Kosambī—who are makers of strife, makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, makers of contention, and makers of legal issues in the Saṅgha—are coming to Sāvatthī.”
“Venerable sir, how should I conduct myself toward those bhikkhus?
“In that case, Rāhula, you should stand in accordance with the Dhamma.
“But venerable sir, how shall I know what is the Dhamma and what is not the Dhamma?”
“Rāhula, one who speaks contrary to the Dhamma should be known by eighteen grounds.
Here, Rāhula, a bhikkhu proclaims what is contrary to the Dhamma as the Dhamma, and what is the Dhamma as contrary to the Dhamma;
he proclaims what is contrary to the Vinaya as the Vinaya, and what is the Vinaya as contrary to the Vinaya.”

He proclaims what was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as having been spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata, and he proclaims what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata as not having been spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata.
He proclaims what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as having been practiced by the Tathāgata, and he proclaims what was practiced by the Tathāgata as not having been practiced by the Tathāgata.
He proclaims what was not laid down by the Tathāgata as having been laid down by the Tathāgata, and he proclaims what was laid down by the Tathāgata as not having been laid down by the Tathāgata.
He explains what is not an offense as an offense, and what is an offense as not an offense;
he explains a light offense as a heavy offense, and a heavy offense as a light offense;
he explains an offense with remainder as an offense without remainder, and an offense without remainder as an offense with remainder.
To represent a grave offense as a minor offense, and to represent a minor offense as a grave offense—
by these eighteen grounds, Rāhula, one should be known as a speaker of what is not Dhamma.
And by eighteen grounds, Rāhula, one should be known as a speaker of the Dhamma.
"Here, Rāhula, a bhikkhu proclaims what is not Dhamma as 'not Dhamma,' and he proclaims the Dhamma as 'Dhamma';
he proclaims what is not Vinaya as 'not Vinaya,' and he proclaims the Vinaya as 'Vinaya';

he proclaims what has not been spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as 'not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata,' and he proclaims what has been spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata as 'spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata.'"
He proclaims what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as "not practiced by the Tathāgata," and what was practiced by the Tathāgata as "practiced by the Tathāgata";
he proclaims what was not laid down by the Tathāgata as "not laid down by the Tathāgata," and what was laid down by the Tathāgata as "laid down by the Tathāgata";
he proclaims what is not an offense as "not an offense," and what is an offense as "an offense."
He explains a light offense as a light offense; he explains a heavy offense as a heavy offense;
he explains an offense with remainder as an offense with remainder; he explains an offense without remainder as an offense without remainder;
he explains a grave offense as a grave offense; he explains a non-grave offense as a non-grave offense.
“Rāhula, by these eighteen grounds, one who speaks according to the Dhamma is to be known.

8. Discussion on the Concord of the Saṅgha Then those monks who were following the one who had been suspended, having reinstated that suspended monk, approached the monks who had carried out the suspension. Having approached, they said this to the monks who had carried out the suspension:
“Friends, regarding the matter on account of which there was quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute for the Saṅgha, and a schism in the Saṅgha...”
This is a schism in the Saṅgha, a formal division of the Saṅgha, a fracture of the Saṅgha; this very monk has been charged with an offense, suspended, has seen [the offense], and has been reinstated.
Come now, friends, let us effect the reconciliation of the Saṅgha for the sake of settling that matter.”
Then those monks who had suspended [the other monks] approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, those monks said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, those monks who follow those who have been suspended said this:"
“Friends, regarding that matter in which there was for the Saṅgha quarreling, strife, contention, dispute, schism in the Saṅgha, fracture in the Saṅgha,
division of the Saṅgha, and separation of the Saṅgha— that very bhikkhu has committed the offense,
has been suspended, has seen [the offense], and has been reinstated.”
“Come then, friends, let us restore harmony to the Saṅgha for the sake of settling that matter.
“But how, Bhante, should we proceed?
“Bhikkhus, since that bhikkhu has been charged, suspended, seen [his fault], and reinstated, let the Saṅgha, bhikkhus, restore harmony to the Saṅgha for the sake of settling that matter.”
And furthermore, monks, it should be done in this way:
everyone, both those who are ill and those who are not ill, must assemble together in one place.
No one at all should give their consent by proxy.
Having assembled, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.
Regarding that matter in which there arose for the Saṅgha contention, quarreling, strife, dispute, schism in the Saṅgha, and fracture in the Saṅgha...”
The formal establishment of the Saṅgha and the causing of division in the Saṅgha: this monk has committed that offense, has been suspended, has seen [the offense], and has been reinstated.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha effect the reconciliation of the Saṅgha for the sake of settling that matter.
This is the motion.
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
Regarding that matter in which there was quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute for the Saṅgha— namely, the schism of the Saṅgha, the fracture of the Saṅgha, the division of the Saṅgha,
and the separation of the Saṅgha— that very bhikkhu has committed the offense, has been suspended, has seen [the offense], and has been reinstated."
The Saṅgha effects a reconciliation of the Saṅgha for the sake of settling that matter.
Whoever among the Venerable Ones approves of the effecting of this reconciliation of the Saṅgha for the sake of settling that matter, let him be silent; whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The Saṅgha has effected a reconciliation of the Saṅgha for the sake of settling that matter.

“The schism in the Saṅgha has been struck down; the strife in the Saṅgha has been struck down; the formal separation of the Saṅgha has been struck down; the diversity within the Saṅgha has been struck down.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.
At that very moment, the Uposatha should be performed and the Pātimokkha should be recited.
9. Upāli’s Inquiry Concerning the Concord of the Saṅgha Then the Venerable Upāli approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Upāli said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, when there is a matter concerning which the Saṅgha has quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute, a schism in the Saṅgha, a fracture in the Saṅgha,
a division in the Saṅgha, and a separation in the Saṅgha— if the Saṅgha effects concord by not having decided that matter,
but instead goes from the rootless to the root, is that concord of the Saṅgha, venerable sir, legitimate?”
“Upāli, in whatever matter there is quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute for the Saṅgha— resulting in a schism of the Saṅgha,
a fracture of the Saṅgha, a division of the Saṅgha, and a separation of the Saṅgha— if the Saṅgha effects reconciliation without having settled that matter,
without having gone from rootless to the root, that reconciliation of the Saṅgha, Upāli, is unrighteous.”
“But, Bhante, regarding whatever matter there may be in which the Saṅgha has quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute, as well as schism in the Saṅgha,
fracture in the Saṅgha, division in the Saṅgha, and separation in the Saṅgha— if the Saṅgha,
having adjudicated that matter and traced it back to its root, effects harmony in the Saṅgha, is that harmony of the Saṅgha, Bhante, in accordance with the Dhamma?”
“Upāli, in whatever matter there is quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute within the Saṅgha— such as a schism in the Saṅgha,
a fracture in the Saṅgha, a division of the Saṅgha, or a separation of the Saṅgha— if the Saṅgha,
having adjudicated that matter and traced it back to its root, effects harmony in the Saṅgha, that, Upāli, is a legitimate harmony of the Saṅgha.”
“How many kinds of harmony in the Saṅgha are there, venerable sir?
“There are these two kinds of harmony in the Saṅgha, Upāli:
harmony that possesses the purpose but lacks the phrasing, and harmony that possesses both the purpose and the phrasing.”
Upāli, there is concord of the Saṅgha that is endowed with both meaning and phrasing.
And what, Upāli, is concord of the Saṅgha that is endowed with meaning but deficient in phrasing?
It is that, Upāli, regarding whatever matter there is quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute within the Saṅgha, leading to a schism in the Saṅgha.
A schism in the Saṅgha, a formal division of the Saṅgha, a separation of the Saṅgha;

when the Saṅgha, without having decided that matter, goes from rootlessness to a root and effects concord in the Saṅgha—this, Upāli, is called concord in the Saṅgha that possesses the meaning but lacks the phrasing.
And what, Upāli, is concord in the Saṅgha that possesses both the meaning and the phrasing?
"Upāli, in whatever matter there is quarreling, arguing, contention, and dispute within the Saṅgha— such as a schism in the Saṅgha,
a fracture in the Saṅgha, a division of the Saṅgha, or a separation of the Saṅgha— if the Saṅgha,
having adjudicated that matter and traced it back to its root, brings about concord in the Saṅgha, this, Upāli, is called concord in the Saṅgha that is endowed with both meaning and phrasing."
“These, Upāli, are the two kinds of harmony within the Saṅgha.
Then the Venerable Upāli rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“In matters concerning the Saṅgha and in its deliberations...”
When matters have arisen and legal disputes have occurred,
how does a man here who seeks the great goal conduct himself?
And how does a bhikkhu here become one worthy of support?
“Blameless in conduct through the first virtue,
observing proper behavior with well-restrained faculties,
his adversaries do not reproach him on account of the Dhamma.”
For there is nothing by which they could speak against him.
Established in such purity of virtue,
he is confident and speaks with assurance.
He does not tremble when gone into an assembly, nor does he falter;
he does not fail in his purpose while speaking with earnest application.
Likewise, when questioned with a question in assemblies, he remains steadfast.
He neither broods nor becomes dejected;
being discerning, he delights the assembly of the wise with his timely words worthy of exposition.
Reverential toward the elder bhikkhus,
confident in his own teacher’s role,
he is capable of measuring [the situation] and skilled in speaking.
Skilled in overcoming adversaries,
he brings those adversaries to subjection,
while the great multitude receives his instruction.
He does not neglect his own livelihood,
yet he provides an answer to a question that is non-harmful;
he is fully capable in the business of acting as a messenger.
And they say of him regarding the duties of the Saṅgha:
"Sent by the assembly of monks, he carries out their word.
Yet he does not think because of that, "I am doing it."
In how many matters one incurs an offense,
and how the emergence from that offense occurs—
these two Vibhaṅgas are well-expounded for both.
He is skilled in the basis for emergence from an offense;
he understands the grounds for sending away, how one is sent away,
and the proper conduct [to be observed] once sent away.
The restoration of a person who has lived [the life]—
this too he knows, being skilled in analysis;
he is respectful toward the elder bhikkhus.
“Among the elders, the middle-ranking, and the novices,
the wise one who acts for the welfare of the great multitude—
that kind of bhikkhu is worthy of support here.”
The Tenth Chapter: The Kosambaka Khandhaka.
Its summary verse:
In Kosambī, the Best of Conquerors...
When seeing that a dispute has arisen,
one should not cast it upon this person or that; rather,
with faith, one should confess the offense.
Within the boundary of Antosīma, right there,
are Bālaka and Vaṃsadā,
as well as Pālileyya and Sāvatthī.
Sāriputta and Kolita;
Mahākassapa and Kaccāna,
Koṭṭhika and Kappina;
Mahācunda and Anuruddha,
Revata and Upāli both,
Ānanda and Rāhula as well—
Gotamī and Nāthapiṇḍika provided secluded lodgings as well as equal offerings of material requisites.
No one should give their consent,
as asked by Upāli;
one who is blameless in virtue [should do so].
“Harmony is the teaching of the Conqueror.
The Kosalamba Khandhaka is finished.
